Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Staff Sgt. Cody Reeves has survived harrowing conditions and stared down enemies on the battlefield during two tours in the military hotspots of Iraq. Staff. Sgt. Cody Reeves works out with his fellow Old Guard soldiers. Now he is stationed near Dover Air Force Base in Delaware, trained to carry the remains of fellow soldiers who perished in that same conflict. Before,"it was all about catching the bad guy," Reeves said. "When you come here, it's all about honoring your brothers who are fallen for catching the bad guys, for their service." Reeves serves in the Army's Old Guard, a tight-knit group of soldiers of similar height and size who physically bear the weight of the Army's fallen veterans. The Old Guard conducts a 15-minute ceremony called a dignified transfer. A recent decision by Defense Secretary Robert Gates gives families the choice to allow media to film the solemn event. It's the first time in 20 years the ceremony has been open to the press.  Watch members of the Old Guard in action » . Every detail of the transfer is precise. When an American soldier dies overseas, the Old Guard is called into action. They travel from their base to Dover, where they meet the aircraft carrying the soldier's body. The six men receive the flag-draped casket, which can weigh 500 pounds, and carry the soldier's body to a waiting vehicle. Women serve as officers in charge on the Army transfer teams, but do not carry the caskets. For Air Force transfers, which use eight people, women help carry the coffin. Despite the cold or the heat, the late hour when the planes often arrive and the physical and emotional strain of their job, the soldiers keep their faces blank. "There's definitely times where your mind goes off, even in the ceremony," said Spc. Wilbert Steinborn, another member of the Old Guard. "You say, 'This guy might have a wife or kids or mother or father who's never going to see him again.' "You can't let it show. Inside you might feel it, and definitely a human's going to feel that -- they're going to feel that emotion. But you can't show that on the outside," Steinborn said. The men stifle sneezes, learn to yawn through their noses and betray no sign of the burden they carry. And -- what they say makes keeping their composure even more important -- the team performs its duties in front of the soldiers' families. "We're soldiers too. We're infantrymen. We could easily be in their place," Steinborn said. "It's hard because you honestly think you see your wife or your girlfriend sitting where the next-of-kin is. You can imagine yourself being there.... So I think that's why we try to be as precise and exact, and look as good, and make them look as good as possible." Some of the Old Guard choose to learn about the lives of the soldiers they've carried. Reeves asks for information about the fallen after having participated in the ceremonies, but never before he greets the soldier's body. "It's 'take care of business' and then afterwards I like to know a little bit about the soldier," he said. "That way you can keep emotions at bay and you're just focused on doing the soldier part." Strikingly, the men, who head to their barracks' gym for intense weight training twice a day and take five-mile runs as a team, seem to be able to communicate without speaking. After drilling for countless hours on the base's grounds, they can feel if another man is even minutely out of step in the ceremony. Sometimes they'll whisper corrections so discreetly no onlooker would ever notice. The nature of their job means the men also share a tighter, unspoken bond. "When I was walking through the aircraft and saw the transfer case with the American flag draped over it, it was -- it was very emotional," Steinborn said. "I don't know if it sadness or pride or what, but -- it was honestly the most difficult and touching thing that I have ever done."

WASHINGTON (CNN) — During two deployments to Iraq, Staff Sgt. Cody Reeves endured dangerous conditions and confronted enemy forces. Today, he serves near Delaware’s Dover Air Force Base, where he has been trained to carry the remains of service members killed in the conflict in which he once fought.

Reeves, who trains alongside other soldiers in the Old Guard, said his mission in Iraq centered on pursuing the enemy. His current responsibility, by contrast, is to pay tribute to fellow troops who died while carrying out that mission and serving their country.

He belongs to the Army’s Old Guard, a close-knit unit whose members are matched by height and build. Together, they shoulder the physical weight of fallen Army personnel.

The unit performs a carefully choreographed, 15-minute ritual known as a dignified transfer. Under a recent policy change ordered by Defense Secretary Robert Gates, relatives may decide whether news organizations can record the solemn proceedings. The decision opened the ceremony to media coverage for the first time in two decades.

Every movement during a transfer must be exact. When a U.S. soldier is killed abroad, Old Guard members leave their base and travel to Dover, where they await the plane bringing the service member home. A six-man team receives the casket, covered by an American flag and sometimes weighing as much as 500 pounds, then carries it to a waiting vehicle.

Women serve as the officers overseeing the Army’s transfer teams, although they do not carry the caskets. Air Force transfer teams consist of eight people, and women may help bear the coffin.

The aircraft often arrive late at night. Regardless of extreme cold, intense heat, exhaustion, or the emotional and physical demands of the assignment, team members must maintain expressionless faces.

Spc. Wilbert Steinborn, also a member of the Old Guard, said thoughts can wander even while the ceremony is underway. A soldier may find himself thinking about the dead service member’s spouse, children, parents, and the reality that they will never see their loved one again.

Those feelings are natural, Steinborn said, but they cannot be visible. The soldiers suppress sneezes, practice yawning through their noses, and avoid displaying any outward indication of the load they are carrying.

Maintaining control is especially important because the fallen troops’ relatives are present as the team performs its work.

Steinborn noted that Old Guard members are soldiers and infantrymen themselves and could easily have suffered the same fate. At times, he said, a man may look toward the next of kin and imagine his own wife or girlfriend sitting there. That possibility drives the team to execute every movement with precision, present themselves impeccably, and honor the fallen as respectfully as possible.

Some Old Guard soldiers later seek information about the people whose remains they have carried. Reeves asks about each fallen soldier only after the ceremony, never before receiving the body. He said separating the task from the personal details helps him control his emotions and concentrate fully on his military duty. Once the work is finished, he wants to learn something about the individual he helped bring home.

The team’s coordination can appear almost wordless. Its members complete strenuous weight-training sessions twice each day in their barracks gym and run five miles together. After spending countless hours practicing on base, they can sense when another bearer is even slightly out of rhythm. If necessary, they quietly offer corrections in a way that spectators are unlikely to detect.

Their responsibilities also create a particularly strong bond that does not need to be spoken aloud.

Steinborn recalled walking through an aircraft and seeing a transfer case covered by the U.S. flag. The sight affected him deeply. He could not identify whether he felt grief, pride, or a combination of emotions, but he described the experience as both the hardest and most moving duty he had ever performed.

At Dover Air Force Base, the return of a fallen service member is marked by a ceremony of exacting precision. Members of the Army’s Old Guard move in carefully rehearsed formation as they approach the aircraft, lift the flag-draped transfer case, and carry it toward a waiting vehicle. Every step, turn, and hand placement is controlled. The purpose is not pageantry, but dignity: to ensure that those who died in service to the country are received with solemnity and respect.

The ceremony is known as a “dignified transfer.” It often takes place far from public view, sometimes late at night or in harsh weather, shortly after an aircraft carrying remains arrives at Dover. Commands are quiet, movements deliberate, and military decorum absolute. The service members performing the transfer must remain composed regardless of rain, wind, fatigue, or the weight they carry.

That burden is both physical and emotional. The transfer team must maneuver in close coordination, keeping the case level and the flag undisturbed. A single member falling out of step can affect the entire formation, so the teams train repeatedly until their movements become instinctive. Yet no amount of practice can make the meaning of the duty routine. Inside each transfer case is a fellow service member being returned home, often with grieving relatives nearby.

The troops are expected to acknowledge that reality without allowing emotion to disrupt the ceremony. They may know little about the fallen person, or they may recognize details that make the loss feel painfully close to their own lives. Either way, their responsibility is the same: to provide a final act of military fellowship and to carry out the family’s first formal welcome home.

For two decades, the public rarely saw these moments. Media coverage of returning war dead was prohibited, a policy intended in part to protect families’ privacy but criticized for shielding the human cost of war from view. Under a new policy, relatives may now authorize news organizations to attend and document a dignified transfer. If a family does not give permission, the ceremony remains private.

The change places control with the families while opening a narrow window onto a ritual previously witnessed mainly by military personnel and loved ones. Photographs and video show no battlefield and offer no account of how a service member died. Instead, they capture the measured steps of the carry team, the folded edges of the flag, the waiting vehicle, and the silence surrounding the return.

For the public, such images can make distant conflicts more immediate. Casualty figures become connected to individual lives, grieving families, and the service members entrusted with bringing the dead home. The coverage also reveals the discipline required of the transfer teams, whose role demands that they absorb the gravity of the moment while showing almost none of their own distress.

At Dover, the ceremony remains focused on the fallen and the family, whether cameras are present or not. The Old Guard’s movements do not change, nor does the standard it must meet. Each transfer is carried out with the same precision, restraint, and reverence—a final journey completed by those who understand both the honor of the duty and its cost.

### Army Old Guard soldiers honor fallen service members during dignified transfers at Dover

**DOVER AIR FORCE BASE, Delaware —** In the stillness of the flight line, soldiers assigned to the Army’s 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment, known as “The Old Guard,” carry out one of the military’s most solemn responsibilities: bringing fallen service members home with dignity.

During a dignified transfer at Dover Air Force Base, a specially trained carry team moves a flag-draped transfer case from an arriving military aircraft to a waiting vehicle. Every step is deliberate, reflecting the military’s commitment to honor those who died while serving the United States.

Dover is home to Air Force Mortuary Affairs Operations, the Defense Department’s primary facility for receiving and caring for service members who die overseas. Personnel there coordinate with each military branch, whose members may provide carry teams representing the fallen service member’s branch of service.

For Old Guard soldiers, best known for ceremonial duties in the Washington area and at Arlington National Cemetery, the mission demands precision, composure and respect. Team members train repeatedly to ensure their movements remain synchronized under emotionally difficult circumstances.

The transfers are often attended by senior military leaders and, when families choose to be present, loved ones of the deceased. Media access and the release of photographs are governed by the wishes of the families.

No speeches are delivered on the flight line. Commands are kept to a minimum. The focus remains on the fallen and on ensuring their return is handled with care.

The ceremony is brief, but its meaning extends far beyond the runway. For the soldiers entrusted with the task, each dignified transfer represents a final act of service to a fellow member of the armed forces—and a promise that their sacrifice will not be forgotten.

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a feature story on Staff Sgt. Cody Reeves and the emotional discipline required to carry flag-draped caskets returning from Iraq.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Weight of Coming Home**

The flag-draped casket does not sway.

That is the first responsibility Staff Sgt. Cody Reeves and the other members of the carry team accept as they approach the aircraft: Keep it level. Match the cadence. Make every movement deliberate.

Inside is an American service member returning from Iraq. Nearby, military leaders, family members and fellow troops may be watching. Cameras may record the dignified transfer, but the ceremony is not performed for them. It is for the fallen and for those left behind.

Reeves takes his place beside the transfer case. Commands are spare and precise. White-gloved hands secure their grip. Together, the team lifts.

In that moment, emotion must yield to discipline.

The service members who perform dignified transfers are not expected to be without feeling. The duty demands the opposite: They must understand the significance of what they carry while refusing to let grief disrupt the mission. A faltering step, an uneven lift or a distracted glance would intrude on a family’s final memory of a loved one’s return.

So Reeves focuses on what can be controlled—the pressure of his hands, the pace of the team, the distance to the waiting vehicle.

Each step is measured. No one rushes.

The American flag stretched across the case transforms the movement from transportation into ceremony. Its presence declares that the fallen did not return as cargo. They returned in the custody of their country, attended by service members entrusted with bringing them home honorably.

For Reeves, that trust carries its own weight.

The wars in Iraq and Afghanistan made dignified transfers a recurring image of military sacrifice: an aircraft open to the night, a carry team moving in formation, a flag bright beneath floodlights. Repetition, however, does not make the work routine. Every case represents one life and one circle of people permanently changed.

That knowledge must be acknowledged—but, for a time, held at a distance.

Emotional discipline is often mistaken for emotional absence. In military service, it is more accurately the ability to decide when feeling can surface. During the transfer, grief is contained within posture and protocol. Reeves’ bearing becomes a form of respect. The straight back, synchronized steps and fixed attention say what the team cannot pause to put into words: *You are not alone. You will be carried with care.*

The physical task is shared. So is the strain.

Carry-team members depend on one another to maintain balance and cadence. If one person moves too quickly, everyone feels it. If one grip shifts, the others compensate. The unity visible in the ceremony is also practical—a group assuming a burden that should not fall on any one person.

When the team reaches the transfer vehicle, it moves with the same controlled precision. The case is positioned, lowered and released only on command. Hands withdraw together. The service members step back.

The transfer may last only minutes. Its emotional aftermath can last much longer.

There is no dramatic release on the flight line. Reeves cannot collapse into reflection while the duty remains unfinished. The team must clear the area, account for equipment and prepare for whatever comes next. Only later, away from the ceremony, can the person beneath the uniform begin to absorb what the uniform required.

That separation is never complete. Details remain: the silence between commands, the feel of the handle through a glove, the flag pulled taut, the knowledge that a family is waiting.

Yet Reeves returns when called.

He does so because dignity depends on people willing to master their own emotions without denying them—people who can carry sorrow steadily, one synchronized step at a time.

The casket does not sway.

The fallen service member comes home.

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe the military’s dignified transfer ceremony, including the Old Guard’s training, precise procedures, physical demands, and interactions with grieving families.
counterfactuals.output:
A **dignified transfer** is the solemn movement of a fallen U.S. service member’s remains from an arriving military aircraft into the care of the Air Force Mortuary Affairs Operations center at Dover Air Force Base, Delaware. It is not a funeral and normally includes no speeches, music, or ceremonial volleys. Its purpose is the quiet, respectful return of the deceased to U.S. soil.

### The transfer procedure

Before the aircraft arrives, a specially trained **carry team**—normally drawn from the fallen member’s service—rehearses the movement and receives instructions specific to the aircraft, transfer case, route, and weather. The team forms near the aircraft while senior military leaders, a chaplain, mortuary personnel, and any attending relatives stand in designated positions.

After the aircraft stops and is secured:

1. The cargo door or ramp opens.
2. The carry team approaches in formation.
3. Members carefully receive the flag-draped transfer case.
4. Moving in exact cadence and maintaining level alignment, they carry it along a predetermined route.
5. They place it into a waiting mortuary transfer vehicle.
6. The team renders honors and withdraws only after the vehicle is prepared to depart.

Commands and movements are deliberately limited. Team members maintain composure, avoid unnecessary eye contact or gestures, and treat the transfer case as the physical presence of the fallen service member. Procedures may be adjusted for aircraft configuration, team size, operational circumstances, or safety, but dignity and control remain paramount.

### The Old Guard and ceremonial training

The Army’s **3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment, “The Old Guard,”** is best known for conducting Army funerals and other ceremonies in the Washington, D.C., area, particularly at Arlington National Cemetery. Dover dignified transfers are generally performed by service-specific carry teams rather than exclusively by the Old Guard, although the standards share the same ceremonial principles.

Old Guard soldiers undergo intensive training in:

- Casket and transfer-case handling  
- Marching cadence and formation alignment  
- Precise turns, lifts, lowers, and hand placements  
- Flag folding and presentation  
- Rifle volleys and other funeral honors, when assigned  
- Uniform preparation and ceremonial bearing  
- Working silently as a team under emotionally difficult conditions  

Training relies on repeated drills, often with weighted practice caskets. Every step, grip, pause, and change of direction is rehearsed until members can respond together without visible hesitation. Soldiers are also taught contingency procedures for uneven ground, narrow spaces, bad weather, equipment problems, or a teammate losing balance.

### Physical demands

The work is physically taxing. A transfer case or casket may be heavy, and the weight can vary considerably. Team members must support it evenly while walking slowly, sometimes down aircraft ramps, across wet or icy pavement, or over cemetery terrain. They may have to hold a stationary position for extended periods while wearing formal uniforms in intense heat, cold, wind, or rain.

Strength alone is insufficient. The job demands:

- Grip and shoulder endurance  
- Balance and synchronized footwork  
- Controlled breathing  
- The ability to remain motionless  
- Precise movement despite fatigue, weather, or emotion  

Teams practice lifting together so no member jerks, readjusts visibly, or causes the case or casket to tilt.

### Interactions with grieving families

Families may attend a dignified transfer, but attendance is voluntary. They are usually briefed beforehand by casualty-assistance and mortuary personnel, told where to stand, and supported throughout by chaplains or assigned family representatives. Ceremonial personnel generally do not initiate conversation during the transfer; their respect is communicated through discipline, bearing, and careful handling.

Privacy is closely protected. Media coverage at Dover is permitted only under established rules and generally depends on the family’s consent. Officials attempt to shield relatives from administrative burdens and avoid intruding on private grief.

At a funeral, interactions may be more direct. A ceremonial representative may present the folded flag to the next of kin and offer a prescribed expression of the nation’s gratitude. Honor-guard members are trained to speak clearly and compassionately while maintaining military formality. They are also taught that families may cry, reach toward the casket, hesitate, or react unpredictably; the team’s role is to remain calm, patient, and unobtrusive.

The defining principle in both dignified transfers and funeral honors is that technical precision serves a human purpose: honoring the fallen while giving the family a final experience of care, order, and respect.

**WASHINGTON —** The Pentagon has allowed news organizations to cover the return of a fallen service member at Dover Air Force Base for the first time in nearly 20 years, ending a long-standing prohibition on photographing flag-draped transfer cases arriving in the United States.

Media representatives were permitted to witness the dignified transfer of Air Force Staff Sgt. Phillip Myers, 30, of Hopewell, Virginia, after his family granted permission. Myers died from wounds suffered in a roadside bombing in Afghanistan.

The coverage followed a policy change announced by Defense Secretary Robert Gates. Under the new rules, families decide whether the media may attend the arrival of their loved one’s remains. If permission is given, journalists can observe from a designated area under restrictions intended to preserve the solemnity of the transfer.

The previous policy, imposed during the 1991 Persian Gulf War, generally barred media coverage of returning war dead at Dover, the military’s principal mortuary facility. Pentagon officials had said the restriction protected the privacy of grieving families, while critics argued that it obscured the human cost of war.

Officials said the revised policy seeks to balance public access with the wishes of relatives. Families that decline coverage will continue to receive privacy, and the Pentagon will not release images from those transfers.

The return of Myers marked the first test of the new approach and offered Americans a rare view of service members carrying a flag-covered transfer case from a military aircraft in a carefully choreographed nighttime ceremony.
